title: Pakistan’s Opposition on the March
gist: Supporters of jailed former Pakistani PM Imran Khan are marching on Islamabad, forcing a government already juggling energy shortages, border tensions and Iran-war mediation to choose between force and concession, while Khan's deteriorating health raises the risk of destabilizing unrest. The brief also covers protests against India's election commissioner, Pakistan's troop deployment to Saudi Arabia under the Mecca pact, and the World Bank's estimate of Nepal's flood damage.

insights.claim: Supporters of Imran Khan's PTI, Pakistan's main opposition party, began a long march from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa toward Islamabad in October 2026 to pressure the government to free Khan, who has been jailed for more than three years.
insights.speaker: Michael Kugelman
insights.so_what: Renewed mass mobilization signals elevated political-instability risk in a nuclear-armed, IMF-dependent state.
insights.quote: Pakistan’s government is facing one of its most serious political challenges in months as supporters of jailed former Prime Minister Imran Khan march toward the capital, Islamabad.

insights.claim: Pakistani streets had been relatively quiet since protests after Khan's August 2023 arrest and the February 2024 elections because repression and arrests of PTI leaders made mobilization difficult, but anger in Khan's base has grown as he remains in prison.

insights.so_what: Suppressed grievances can re-emerge abruptly, so a period of calm understated latent unrest risk.

insights.claim: Khan's family says his health is worsening, and Pakistan flouted a Supreme Court order in August to move him to a private medical facility, taking him instead for a brief stay at a public hospital.

insights.claim: If Imran Khan died in custody, even of natural causes, his supporters would blame the state, which could trigger massive, destabilizing protests in Pakistan.
insights.speaker: Michael Kugelman
insights.so_what: Khan's death in custody is a low-probability, high-impact tail risk for Pakistani stability.
insights.quote: If Khan suffered that fate, even if by natural causes, his support base would blame the state, which could result in massive, destabilizing protests.

insights.claim: The author speculates Pakistani officials may have offered Khan exile or house arrest in exchange for silence, but judges he is unlikely to accept such a deal.
insights.speaker: Michael Kugelman
insights.so_what: An easy off-ramp for the standoff appears unlikely, prolonging political risk.
insights.quote: Never one to defer, the former leader is unlikely to accept such an offer.

insights.claim: Protests across India are demanding that Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar resign over voter-roll changes, after an Indian Express report found the revision campaign begun in 2024 was rife with improprieties.
insights.speaker: Michael Kugelman
insights.so_what: Challenges to electoral-institution credibility add a governance risk to the India investment narrative.

insights.claim: The Cockroach Janta Party, which earlier forced Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan to resign, leads the youth-driven protest movement, which the author calls a gift to India's weak opposition that has struggled to capitalize on Modi's vulnerabilities such as entrenched youth unemployment.
insights.speaker: Michael Kugelman
insights.so_what: Youth unemployment is becoming a political liability for Modi, potentially eroding the stability premium priced into India.
insights.quote: This week’s protests, and the Cockroach movement on the whole, are a gift to a weak Indian opposition.

insights.claim: Pakistan and Turkey announced they will deploy troops to Saudi Arabia to counter Houthi attacks under the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement signed in August, which treats an attack on one member as an attack on all three.
insights.speaker: Michael Kugelman
insights.so_what: First invocation of a NATO-style Gulf-South Asia pact changes the security calculus around Saudi oil infrastructure.

insights.claim: Deploying troops to Saudi Arabia risks dragging Pakistan into a Middle East war and costing it credibility with Iran as a neutral mediator.
insights.speaker: Michael Kugelman
insights.so_what: Loss of a credible mediator could prolong Iran-related conflict risk premia in energy markets.
insights.quote: For Pakistan, the decision carries some risk: It doesn’t want to be dragged into a Middle East war, and it risks losing credibility in the eyes of Iran as a neutral mediator.

insights.claim: A World Bank report found Nepal's August floods damaged or destroyed more than 10 percent of the country's installed hydropower and solar capacity, including 12 hydropower projects.
insights.speaker: Michael Kugelman
insights.so_what: Climate shocks to hydropower affect Nepal's power exports and regional energy-trade assumptions.
insights.quote: More than 10 percent of Nepal’s installed hydropower and solar capacity, including 12 hydropower projects, was damaged or destroyed.
insights.locator: The economic impact of Nepal’s floods

insights.claim: About two-thirds of a key 50-mile Nepal trade corridor was damaged in the floods, and the World Bank forecasts Nepal's real GDP growth falling to 3.7 percent in fiscal 2027 from a projected 3.9 percent in fiscal 2026.
insights.speaker: Michael Kugelman
insights.so_what: Quantifies the growth drag from climate disasters on a fragile frontier economy.
insights.quote: The World Bank forecasts that Nepal’s real GDP growth for fiscal year 2027 will fall to 3.7 percent, compared with a projected 3.9 percent for fiscal year 2026.
